svg.title: Federation Trust Evaluation
svg.desc: How Operator A decides whether it may federate with Operator B under the BANZA protocol, using only verifiable evidence. At the top, Operator A is the evaluating operator and Operator B is an independent target operator that self-publishes its operator manifest, signed protocol metadata and conformance evidence. Between them sits the Open Trust Evaluation: ten ordered checks, evaluated in sequence, automated, deterministic and reproducible by anyone. Two sources of trust material feed the chain. The Public Protocol Registry is a verifiable index of protocol metadata and evidence; it is not a list of operators licensed, approved or certified by BANZA, and absence from the registry is not a regulatory prohibition. The Trust Root and its delegated signing keys sign protocol metadata, releases, delegated keys and revocations; the Trust Root does not authorise operators, does not authorise payments, issues no licence and moves no funds. The ordered chain runs downward: check one, the operator manifest is valid, well formed and self-published by Operator B; check two, the declared protocol version is compatible with Operator A; check three, the protocol metadata is signed and the signature verifies; check four, conformance evidence is present, complete and valid; check five, the signature chain from trust root to delegated key verifies; check six, the operator metadata resolves in the public protocol registry; check seven, the key and metadata are not present in the revocation list; check eight, the requested capabilities are declared and compatible; check nine, the endpoint contract is compatible with the protocol version; check ten, the evidence is within the freshness window set by policy. Each check passes downward to the next one along the spine. Every check also has a red exit to the right into the fail-closed rail: trust material that is missing, invalid, expired, revoked or incompatible stops the evaluation immediately and federation routing does not start. Fail-closed is the default exit of every check, not an exception; the chain must positively verify all ten checks before routing may begin, absence of evidence is not trust, and there is no override. Revocation is a protocol security signal: the Revocation List is a security and trust mechanism, not a licence, a regulatory sanction or a financial authorisation. When all ten checks verify, federation routing is enabled between Operator A and Operator B. Between the passing chain and enabled routing there is a position where a central approval step would sit; it is drawn as an empty dashed slot and is intentionally empty. No certificate is consulted anywhere in the chain and no human decides the outcome. Every routing decision re-evaluates the chain, and expired, revoked or incompatible trust material returns the decision to fail-closed.

BANZA is an open financial protocol. Operator participation is demonstrated by verifiable protocol conformance, not by central human approval.
Trust is verified by evidence, not human approval.
